unit.unitOverview: Almost everything you say about your ordinary life uses one tense and a handful of small words. This unit teaches the present simple for things that happen regularly, the words that say how often, how to tell the time in both the way it is written and the way it is said, and the three little prepositions that go in front of a time. By the end you can describe your week to someone, and read a shift rota without misreading the one line that matters.
unit.learningPath:
Read and listen to the Lesson. It covers all four patterns.
Open Patterns. Card 2 is short and card 3 has the most to remember.
Learn the words. Twenty-nine, in five groups.
Read the three texts aloud. The third is a shift rota.
Do the Practice. Practice 3 needs a clock or a phone in front of you.
Record yourself describing your own week, and play it back.
Take the quiz, then update My progress.

visual.lectureScript:
This unit is about your ordinary life — what you do most days, and when.
Four patterns.
The first is the present simple, and this is the tense English uses for anything regular. Not what is happening now. What happens generally.
I start work at seven. She finishes at three. We walk to the market on Saturdays.
None of those are happening at this moment. They are what usually happens, and that is exactly what the present simple is for.
You already know the form, because you learned it in Unit 3: the verb stays plain, except for he, she and it, which add s. I start, she starts. We finish, he finishes.
What is new here is the use. Use it for routine, for habit, for timetables, and for facts that stay true. If you can put the word usually in front of it and the sentence still makes sense, the present simple is the right tense.
Second pattern: how often. Always, usually, often, sometimes, never.
These have a fixed position and it surprises people. They go BEFORE the main verb. I always start at seven. She never works on Sundays. We sometimes walk.
Not: I start always at seven. The word comes first.
But there is one exception, and it is the verb you use most. With am, is and are, the word goes AFTER. I am always late. She is never here on Fridays.
So: before an ordinary verb, after am, is or are. Two positions, one exception, and you will use it constantly.
And notice never is already negative. I never work on Sunday. Not I do not never work — English uses one negative, not two.
Third pattern: telling the time. There are two systems and you need both.
Written, you will usually see numbers: 09:40, 14:20, 18:00. This is the twenty-four hour clock and it appears on timetables, appointment cards and rotas.
Spoken, people mostly use twelve. So 14:20 is written as fourteen twenty and said as twenty past two. And 18:00 is said as six o'clock.
The spoken system has a few pieces. On the hour: six o'clock. After the hour, up to thirty minutes: ten past six, quarter past six, half past six. After thirty minutes, you count backwards to the next hour: twenty to seven, quarter to seven.
That backwards part is the one that takes practice, because half the day is expressed by counting down to an hour that has not arrived yet.
A shortcut that always works: read the numbers. Six forty is understood everywhere and nobody minds. Use it while you build the other system.
Fourth pattern: the three small words that go before a time. At, on, in.
At for a clock time: at seven, at half past four, at midnight.
On for a day or a date: on Monday, on Saturday, on the fourteenth of March.
In for a longer period: in the morning, in March, in the winter, in two hours.
The rough shape is that the more precise the time, the shorter the word. At is the most exact, on is a day, in is everything longer.
And three that take no preposition at all: today, tomorrow, yesterday. You say I start tomorrow, never on tomorrow.
Go to Patterns.

readings.title: An Ordinary Tuesday
readings.passageScript:
I wake at half past five. I do not get up straight away — I lie there for ten minutes and listen to the building waking up.
I get up at twenty to six. I never have breakfast at home. There is no time, and I am not hungry that early.
I leave at ten past six and I walk to the bus stop. The journey takes forty minutes, and it is always the same forty minutes, because the traffic is the same every morning.
I start at seven. The first two hours are the busiest, and then it gets quieter.
We have a break at eleven. I have my breakfast then, four hours late, and I study for the last ten minutes of it.
Lunch is at midday. Half an hour.
I finish at three. I am usually home by four, and that is the best part of the day, because nobody wants anything from me until the children come in.
I study in the evening, from eight until half past. Not always. Usually.
I go to bed before eleven. I never sleep well on Sunday nights, and I have never worked out why.

readings.title: The Time, Written and Said
readings.passageScript:
English uses two systems for the time, and you need both, because one is what you read and the other is what you hear.
Written, on timetables, rotas and appointment cards, you will usually see the twenty-four hour clock. 09:40. 14:20. 18:00. 23:15.
Spoken, most people use twelve hours and a set of words.
On the hour: six o'clock.
After the hour, up to thirty minutes: five past six, ten past six, quarter past six, twenty past six, half past six.
After thirty minutes, English counts backwards towards the next hour: twenty-five to seven, twenty to seven, quarter to seven, five to seven.
That backwards half is what takes practice. For half of every hour, English names an hour that has not arrived yet. Quarter to seven is 06:45 — the word seven appears, but it is still six o'clock.
The word o'clock is only used on the exact hour. Six o'clock, yes. Half past six o'clock, no.
And here is the shortcut, which you should use freely while you build the rest. You can always just read the numbers. Six forty-five. Fourteen twenty. Everybody understands it, nobody thinks it is strange, and it is what most people say when they are giving a time quickly.
Use the numbers when you need to be understood. Practise the words when you have time to think. Both are correct.

grammar.title: The present simple: what happens generally
grammar.explanation: This is the tense for anything regular — routine, habit, timetables, and things that stay true. It is not for what is happening at this moment.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
I start        We start
You start      They start
He starts
She starts
It starts

Negative: I do not start. He does not start.
Question: Do you start? Does she start?

Use it for:
  routine ....... I start at seven.
  habit ......... She walks to work.
  timetables .... The bus leaves at ten.
  things that stay true ... The shop closes at six.
grammar.workedExample:
Is the present simple right here: I ____ (work) at the depot?
1. Ask: is this happening at this exact moment, or is it generally true?
2. Generally true — it is where I work, not what I am doing now.
3. So the present simple is right.
4. The subject is I, so no s: work.
Result: I work at the depot.
The test that always works: put usually in front. I usually work at the depot makes sense, so the present simple fits.
grammar.commonMistake: Dropping the s for he, she and it is the usual slip, and it survives because nothing is lost — she start at seven is perfectly clear. The other error is using this tense for right now: I work at the moment should be I am working. If usually fits, use the present simple; if now fits, do not.
grammar.memoryTip: If usually fits in front of it, the present simple is right.
grammar.practice:
Write the correct form.
1. I ____ (start) at seven.
2. She ____ (finish) at three.
3. The bus ____ (leave) at ten past six.
4. We ____ (walk) to the market on Saturdays.
5. He ____ (not work) on Sundays.
6. ____ you ____ (catch) the early bus?
grammar.answerKey:
1. start  2. finishes  3. leaves  4. walk  5. does not work  6. Do … catch
Number 2 adds es rather than s, because finish ends in sh — the same happens with watch, wash and pass.
Numbers 5 and 6 are the ones to check: once do or does appears, the s moves onto it and comes off the main verb.

grammar.title: Always, usually, often, sometimes, never
grammar.explanation: These say how often. They have a fixed position in the sentence, and it is not where most learners first put them.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
BEFORE an ordinary verb:
  I always start at seven.
  She never works on Sundays.
  We sometimes walk.

AFTER am, is, are:
  I am always late.
  She is never here on Fridays.

never is already negative:
  I never work on Sunday.
  NOT: I do not never work.

sometimes can also start a sentence:
  Sometimes the bus does not come.
grammar.workedExample:
Put always into: I start at seven.
1. Find the verb: start.
2. Is it am, is or are? No — it is an ordinary verb.
3. Ordinary verb, so the word goes BEFORE it.
4. I always start at seven.
Now the same word with be: I am late. Here the verb IS am, so the word goes after: I am always late.
One rule, one exception, and the exception is the verb you use most.
grammar.commonMistake: Putting the word at the end — I start at seven always. It is understandable but it sounds wrong to a listener, and the fix is mechanical: find the verb and put the word in front of it, unless the verb is am, is or are.
grammar.memoryTip: Before the verb — unless the verb is be, then after.
grammar.practice:
Put the word in the right place.
1. I start at seven. (always)
2. She is late. (never)
3. We walk to the market. (sometimes)
4. The bus is full. (always)
5. I have breakfast. (never)
6. He works at night. (often)
grammar.answerKey:
1. I always start at seven.
2. She is never late.
3. We sometimes walk to the market. (or: Sometimes we walk to the market.)
4. The bus is always full.
5. I never have breakfast.
6. He often works at night.
Numbers 2 and 4 are the exception — the verb is is, so the word comes after it. The other four all take it before the verb.

grammar.title: Telling the time
grammar.explanation: Two systems. The written one is numbers and appears on rotas, timetables and cards. The spoken one uses words and counts backwards for the second half of every hour.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
On the hour:      six o'clock        06:00
Past the hour:    ten past six       06:10
                  quarter past six   06:15
                  half past six      06:30
To the next hour: twenty to seven    06:40
                  quarter to seven   06:45

o'clock is ONLY for the exact hour.

Always allowed: read the numbers.
  six forty-five · fourteen twenty
grammar.workedExample:
Say 07:50.
1. Are the minutes 30 or less? No — 50.
2. So count backwards to the next hour.
3. 60 minus 50 is 10, so it is ten minutes TO the next hour.
4. The next hour after 7 is 8.
Result: ten to eight.
Notice the number eight appears even though it is still seven o'clock. That is the part to get used to — for half of every hour, English names an hour that has not arrived.
grammar.commonMistake: Two things. Saying half past six o'clock — o'clock belongs only to the exact hour. And using past when the minutes are more than thirty: forty past six should be twenty to seven. If you are unsure, read the numbers instead; that is always correct and nobody minds.
grammar.memoryTip: More than thirty minutes? Count backwards to the next hour.
grammar.practice:
Write these as people say them.
1. 06:00
2. 06:15
3. 06:30
4. 06:45
5. 07:50
Then write these as numbers.
6. quarter past nine
7. twenty to three
grammar.answerKey:
1. six o'clock  2. quarter past six  3. half past six  4. quarter to seven  5. ten to eight
6. 09:15  7. 02:40
Numbers 4, 5 and 7 all cross into the backwards half. In each one the hour named is the NEXT hour, not the current one — quarter to seven is 06:45, and twenty to three is 02:40.

grammar.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
grammar.title: At, on, in before a time
grammar.explanation: Three small words, and which one you use depends only on how precise the time is. The more exact the time, the shorter the word.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
at + a clock time
  at seven · at half past four · at midnight · at night

on + a day or a date
  on Monday · on Saturday · on the fourteenth of March

in + a longer period
  in the morning · in March · in the winter · in two hours

NO preposition:
  today · tomorrow · yesterday · this morning · next week
grammar.workedExample:
Which word: I finish ____ three ____ Friday?
1. First gap: three is a clock time. Clock times take at.
2. Second gap: Friday is a day. Days take on.
Result: I finish at three on Friday.
Now add a third: ... in the afternoon. Afternoon is a longer period, so it takes in. All three in one sentence: I finish at three on Friday afternoon — and notice that once Friday is there, the afternoon attaches to it and the in disappears.
grammar.commonMistake: The two that catch people are at night, which does not follow the pattern (you would expect in the night), and putting a preposition before tomorrow — on tomorrow is wrong, it is just tomorrow. Learn those two as exceptions and the rest follows the rule.
grammar.memoryTip: Exact time — at. A day — on. Anything longer — in.
grammar.practice:
Write at, on, in, or leave it empty.
1. I start ____ seven.
2. The class is ____ Monday.
3. I study ____ the evening.
4. She was born ____ March.
5. He works ____ night.
6. I finish early ____ Friday.
7. See you ____ tomorrow.
8. The appointment is ____ the fourteenth.
grammar.answerKey:
1. at  2. on  3. in  4. in  5. at  6. on  7. (nothing) — tomorrow takes no preposition  8. on
Numbers 5 and 7 are the two exceptions. At night breaks the pattern and simply has to be remembered. Tomorrow, today and yesterday take nothing at all, and adding on is the commonest error on this card.

Describe your ordinary day out loud, in ten sentences, from waking to sleeping.
Every sentence must use the present simple, and at least six must contain a time.

speaking.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

A: What time do you start?

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 1 — Your week, with how often
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write twelve sentences about your week.
Use each of these twice: always, usually, often, sometimes, never, twice.
At least four sentences must use am, is or are, so the frequency word goes after the verb.
Underline the frequency word in every sentence, and circle the verb.
Then check: is the underlined word before the circled one, except where the verb is be?
writing.modelText:
1. I always start at seven.
2. I always walk to the bus stop.
3. I usually have lunch at work.
4. The journey usually takes forty minutes.
5. I often finish late on Mondays.
6. She often works the night shift.
7. I sometimes study on my break.
8. Sometimes the bus does not come.
9. I never have breakfast at home.
10. I never work on Sundays.
11. I am always tired by nine.
12. She is never late.
writing.successCriteria: Twelve sentences; each of the six words used twice; at least four with am, is or are; the frequency word underlined and the verb circled in each; every position correct
writing.support: Write the twelve verbs first, down the page, with nothing else. Then decide which frequency word goes with each. Choosing both at once is what produces sentences where the word drifts to the end.
writing.extension: Rewrite four of them about somebody else, and check what happens to the verb.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 2 — A timetable in sentences
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Write out your own week as a timetable — seven days, with times.
Then write eight sentences describing it, using at, on and in correctly.
At least two sentences must contain all three prepositions.
Underline every preposition of time.
writing.modelText:
Monday 07:00–15:00 · Tuesday 07:00–15:00 · Wednesday free · Thursday 14:00–22:00 · Friday 14:00–22:00 · Saturday 09:00–13:00 · Sunday free
I start at seven on Monday and Tuesday.
On Wednesday I am free all day.
I work the late shift on Thursday and Friday, from two in the afternoon until ten at night.
On Saturday I finish at one.
I never work on Sundays.
I study in the evening on Wednesday.
The class is at six in the evening on Wednesday.
I am busiest in the morning.
writing.expectedLength: A seven-day timetable and eight sentences
writing.successCriteria: Seven days with times; eight sentences; at, on and in each used correctly at least twice; two sentences containing all three; every preposition underlined
writing.support: Write the timetable first and do not write any sentences until it is finished. Describing something that already exists is far easier than inventing the facts and the grammar at the same time.
writing.extension: Add two sentences using today, tomorrow and this evening, with no preposition, and check you did not add one.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 3 — Answer questions from the rota
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Use the shift rota in Reading 3.
Write full-sentence answers to these six questions. Do not answer with one word.
1. When does A. Costa work on Wednesday?
2. Who is on nights all week from Monday to Wednesday?
3. What time does the Friday late shift finish, and why is that unusual?
4. Who is not working at all on Saturday night?
5. If you want to swap a shift, when must it be agreed by?
6. A night shift is listed under Monday. On which evening does it actually start?
writing.modelText:
1. A. Costa works the early shift on Wednesday, from six in the morning until two in the afternoon.
2. R. Iqbal is on nights from Monday to Wednesday.
3. It finishes at eight in the evening, two hours early, because of the early close note for that week only.
4. Nobody is on the night shift on Saturday — the column shows two dashes.
5. By midday on Thursday.
6. It starts on Sunday evening at ten, because a night shift begins the evening before the day it is listed under.
writing.successCriteria: Six answers, each a full sentence; times given correctly; answers 3 and 6 refer to the notes rather than the table; no one-word answers
writing.support: For each question, decide first whether the answer is in the table or in the notes underneath. Three of the six are in the notes, and those are the three that are usually got wrong.
writing.extension: Write your own seventh question — one whose answer requires both the table and a note — and answer it.

writing.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
writing.title: Writing 4 — Correct the eight mistakes
writing.promptAndInstructions:
Every sentence has exactly one mistake from this unit.
Write each out correctly and say which pattern it came from.
1. She start at seven.
2. I start always at seven.
3. It is half past six o'clock.
4. See you on tomorrow.
5. I do not never work on Sundays.
6. The class is at Monday.
7. It is forty past six.
8. She is always late. — I am late always.
writing.modelText:
1. She starts at seven. (Pattern 1 — she takes the s)
2. I always start at seven. (Pattern 2 — the word goes before an ordinary verb)
3. It is half past six. (Pattern 3 — o'clock is only for the exact hour)
4. See you tomorrow. (Pattern 4 — tomorrow takes no preposition)
5. I never work on Sundays. (Pattern 2 — never is already negative)
6. The class is on Monday. (Pattern 4 — a day takes on)
7. It is twenty to seven. (Pattern 3 — past thirty minutes, count backwards)
8. I am always late. (Pattern 2 — after am, is or are, but still not at the end)
writing.successCriteria: All eight corrected; each labelled with the right pattern; no new mistakes introduced
writing.support: Sort them into four piles by pattern before correcting anything. Two are about the verb form, three about word position, two about the clock, and two about prepositions — and once sorted, each card gives the fix.
writing.extension: Look back at Writing 1 and Writing 2 and check every frequency word and every preposition against these eight.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 1 — The present simple
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write the correct form of the verb.
1. I ____ (start) at seven.
2. She ____ (finish) at three.
3. The bus ____ (leave) at ten past six.
4. We ____ (walk) on Saturdays.
5. He ____ (catch) the early train.
6. The shop ____ (close) at midday.
7. They ____ (work) at night.
8. My journey ____ (take) forty minutes.
9. She ____ (not work) on Sundays.
10. ____ you ____ (get up) early?
activities.answerSummary:
1. start  2. finishes  3. leaves  4. walk  5. catches  6. closes  7. work  8. takes  9. does not work  10. Do … get up
Numbers 2 and 5 add es rather than s, because finish and catch end in sh and ch. Number 8 is worth checking — my journey is one thing, so it behaves like it and takes the s.
Eight or more correct means this pattern is working.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 2 — Where does the word go?
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Rewrite each sentence with the word in brackets in the right place.
1. I start at seven. (always)
2. She is late. (never)
3. We walk to the market. (sometimes)
4. The bus is full. (always)
5. I have breakfast. (never)
6. He works at night. (often)
7. I am tired by nine. (usually)
8. The journey takes an hour. (usually)
9. She is here before eight. (never)
10. I study in the evening. (often)
11. It rains in the morning. (sometimes)
12. They are busy on Mondays. (always)
activities.answerSummary:
1. I always start at seven.  2. She is never late.  3. We sometimes walk to the market.  4. The bus is always full.  5. I never have breakfast.  6. He often works at night.  7. I am usually tired by nine.  8. The journey usually takes an hour.  9. She is never here before eight.  10. I often study in the evening.  11. It sometimes rains in the morning.  12. They are always busy on Mondays.
Four of these — 2, 4, 7, 9 and 12 — have be as the verb, so the word goes after it. The other seven take it before. If you got all twelve, the position is now automatic.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 3 — Say the time
activities.instructionsAndItems:
You will need a clock or a phone for the second part.
Part A. Write these as people say them.
1. 07:00  2. 08:15  3. 10:30  4. 12:45  5. 16:50
Part B. Write these as numbers.
6. quarter past nine  7. twenty to three  8. half past eleven  9. five to six
Part C. Look at a clock five times today at random moments. Each time, say the time out loud in the spoken system before you look at the numbers again.
activities.answerSummary:
Part A. 1. seven o'clock  2. quarter past eight  3. half past ten  4. quarter to one  5. ten to five
Part B. 6. 09:15  7. 02:40  8. 11:30  9. 05:55
Watch number 4: 12:45 is quarter to ONE, not quarter to thirteen. Once you cross into the backwards half, you name the next hour on the twelve-hour clock.
Part C has no key — the point is whether you could say it before checking. Most people find the backwards half slow for about a week and then it stops being slow.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 4 — At, on, in, or nothing
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write at, on, in, or leave it empty.
1. I start ____ seven.
2. The class is ____ Monday.
3. I study ____ the evening.
4. She was born ____ March.
5. He works ____ night.
6. I finish early ____ Friday.
7. See you ____ tomorrow.
8. The appointment is ____ the fourteenth.
9. I am busiest ____ the morning.
10. The shift ends ____ midnight.
11. We are free ____ Sunday.
12. I will call you ____ two hours.
13. It is quiet ____ the afternoon.
14. The course starts ____ September.
15. I finished ____ yesterday.
activities.answerSummary:
1. at  2. on  3. in  4. in  5. at  6. on  7. (nothing)  8. on  9. in  10. at  11. on  12. in  13. in  14. in  15. (nothing)
The pattern holds everywhere except two places. Number 5, at night, breaks it and must be remembered. Numbers 7 and 15 take nothing at all — today, tomorrow and yesterday never take a preposition, and adding one is the commonest error here.
Twelve or more correct means this is working.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 5 — Read the rota
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Use the rota in Reading 3.
1. What are the three shift names and their times?
2. Who works early on Monday?
3. Who works late on Wednesday?
4. Which day has nobody working at all?
5. Which day has no night shift?
6. How long is a break, and on which shifts?
7. When must a swap be agreed by?
8. What is different about the Friday late shift this week?
activities.answerSummary:
1. Early 06:00–14:00, Late 14:00–22:00, Night 22:00–06:00  2. A. Costa  3. L. Petrov  4. Sunday  5. Saturday  6. Thirty minutes, on shifts of six hours or more  7. Thursday midday  8. It finishes at 20:00 instead of 22:00, for that week only
Questions 4 and 5 are different and both are easy to confuse: Sunday has nothing at all, while Saturday has an early and a late but no night. Read the dashes carefully — a row of them and a single one mean different things.

activities.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01
activities.title: Practice 6 — Your real week
activities.instructionsAndItems:
Write down what you actually did each day this week — the times you got up, started, finished and slept.
Then write six sentences describing it, using the present simple and frequency words.
Now compare: does what you wrote in the sentences match what actually happened?
If you wrote I always get up at six and you did it four days out of seven, change the word.
activities.answerSummary:
There is no key — it is your week.
What this checks is precision, not English. Learners reach for always and never because they are the easiest words, and end up describing a life they do not lead. Usually means most of the time. Often means many times but not most. Sometimes means a few.
If every sentence you wrote used always or never, go back and make at least three of them more accurate. Saying exactly how often is a real skill and it starts here.

Use at least four different frequency words and at least six times said in the spoken system. Second, write full-sentence answers to the six rota questions in Writing 3, and add a seventh question of your own whose answer needs both the table and one of the notes. Keep both together.

Pushing them towards usually, often and sometimes is worth the time; it is the beginning of saying what is actually the case rather than what is easiest to say.

Numbers 4, 5 and 7 all cross into the backwards half. In each one the hour named is the NEXT hour, not the current one — quarter to seven is 06:45, and twenty to three is 02:40.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. at  2. on  3. in  4. in  5. at  6. on  7. (nothing) — tomorrow takes no preposition  8. on
Numbers 5 and 7 are the two exceptions. At night breaks the pattern and simply has to be remembered. Tomorrow, today and yesterday take nothing at all, and adding on is the commonest error on this card.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. start  2. finishes  3. leaves  4. walk  5. catches  6. closes  7. work  8. takes  9. does not work  10. Do … get up
Numbers 2 and 5 add es rather than s, because finish and catch end in sh and ch. Number 8 is worth checking — my journey is one thing, so it behaves like it and takes the s.
Eight or more correct means this pattern is working.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. I always start at seven.  2. She is never late.  3. We sometimes walk to the market.  4. The bus is always full.  5. I never have breakfast.  6. He often works at night.  7. I am usually tired by nine.  8. The journey usually takes an hour.  9. She is never here before eight.  10. I often study in the evening.  11. It sometimes rains in the morning.  12. They are always busy on Mondays.
Four of these — 2, 4, 7, 9 and 12 — have be as the verb, so the word goes after it. The other seven take it before. If you got all twelve, the position is now automatic.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
Part A. 1. seven o'clock  2. quarter past eight  3. half past ten  4. quarter to one  5. ten to five
Part B. 6. 09:15  7. 02:40  8. 11:30  9. 05:55
Watch number 4: 12:45 is quarter to ONE, not quarter to thirteen. Once you cross into the backwards half, you name the next hour on the twelve-hour clock.
Part C has no key — the point is whether you could say it before checking. Most people find the backwards half slow for about a week and then it stops being slow.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. at  2. on  3. in  4. in  5. at  6. on  7. (nothing)  8. on  9. in  10. at  11. on  12. in  13. in  14. in  15. (nothing)
The pattern holds everywhere except two places. Number 5, at night, breaks it and must be remembered. Numbers 7 and 15 take nothing at all — today, tomorrow and yesterday never take a preposition, and adding one is the commonest error here.
Twelve or more correct means this is working.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
1. Early 06:00–14:00, Late 14:00–22:00, Night 22:00–06:00  2. A. Costa  3. L. Petrov  4. Sunday  5. Saturday  6. Thirty minutes, on shifts of six hours or more  7. Thursday midday  8. It finishes at 20:00 instead of 22:00, for that week only
Questions 4 and 5 are different and both are easy to confuse: Sunday has nothing at all, while Saturday has an early and a late but no night. Read the dashes carefully — a row of them and a single one mean different things.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance:
There is no key — it is your week.
What this checks is precision, not English. Learners reach for always and never because they are the easiest words, and end up describing a life they do not lead. Usually means most of the time. Often means many times but not most. Sometimes means a few.
If every sentence you wrote used always or never, go back and make at least three of them more accurate. Saying exactly how often is a real skill and it starts here.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: finishes — She takes the s, and finish adds es because it ends in sh. Is finishing would mean right now, not every day.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I always start at seven. — The frequency word goes before an ordinary verb. Start is an ordinary verb, so the word comes in front of it.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: She is never late. — With am, is or are the word goes after the verb. This is the one exception to the rule in the previous question.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: quarter to seven — Past thirty minutes English counts backwards to the next hour, so the hour named is seven even though it is still six o'clock.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: It is half past six. — O'clock is used only on the exact hour, so half past six o'clock is wrong. Half past, not half to.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: on — A day takes on. At is for clock times and in is for longer periods like months and seasons.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: no word needed — Today, tomorrow and yesterday take no preposition at all. Adding on is the commonest error on this pattern.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: at — At night is an exception — you would expect in the night from the rule, but English uses at. It simply has to be remembered.
answerKey.reviewStatus: Reviewed: script review and curriculum sign-off, 2026-08-01

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: I never work on Sundays. — Never is already negative. English uses one negative in a sentence, so adding do not makes two.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: 20:00 — The column heading says 22:00, but the note underneath overrides it for that week only. Reading the heading alone gives the wrong answer by two hours.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Sunday 22:00 — The second note says the night shift starts the evening before the day it is listed under. This is the single most misread line on any rota.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Sunday — Sunday shows dashes in all three columns. Saturday has an early and a late shift but no night, which is a different thing.
